stimulus.title: Questions 51 to 55
stimulus.text:
A language class can become very quiet when students are asked to speak without preparation. One teacher, Maria, wondered whether sending discussion questions before class would encourage more useful conversation. She tried the approach with an evening course in which adults often arrived after a full day at work. Each week, students received two questions related to a short reading. They were asked to think about examples, but not to write complete speeches.

During the first few lessons, Maria noticed that more students offered an opening comment. Some brought a few words on a card, while others referred to experiences from their jobs or families. Preparation appeared to reduce the effort needed to begin. Yet a new difficulty soon emerged. A few students prepared long answers and continued speaking even when classmates wanted to respond. The activity risked becoming a series of separate performances rather than a conversation.

Maria adjusted the instructions. Students could prepare one example and two questions to ask a partner. In class, they first listened in pairs and had to ask a follow-up question based on what the other person actually said. They then introduced one interesting idea from their partner to the group. This required attention to someone else's meaning, not simply the delivery of a prepared answer.

Maria did not count every spoken word as evidence of progress. Instead, she kept brief notes on whether students asked relevant questions, clarified confusing points and connected their comments to earlier contributions. These observations helped her decide what to practise next. They did not establish that advance questions would benefit every group.

For Maria, preparation was most useful when it opened a door to interaction. Its value depended on how the classroom task used it. Giving students more time to prepare could help, but the time alone was not a complete teaching method.

questions.solution: In recent years, many cities have opened small public reading spaces in local communities. These places are usually close to people's homes, making them easy to reach on foot. Besides borrowing books, residents can take part in book discussions and storytelling activities for children. Some reading spaces have extended their evening opening hours so that people who are busy at work during the day can also use them. Volunteers help organise books and introduce the services to new readers. Although these spaces are small, they provide places for residents to learn and communicate, and gradually make reading part of everyday community life.

materials.text:
Writing task and assessment knowledge
For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay that begins with the sentence “Learning to question a popular idea is an essential part of education.” You may give examples to support your views. You should write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words. Write your essay on Answer Sheet 1.
A successful essay develops a clear position, explains why popularity alone is insufficient evidence, uses a specific relevant example, and connects independent judgment with responsible evaluation of evidence. Different defensible positions and examples are acceptable.

Listening script · Conversation One
W: You look worried, Ben. Did the community foundation reject our repair café proposal?
M: No, they actually liked the idea. But before releasing the grant, they want evidence that the café changes what people do, rather than simply attracting visitors.
W: We recorded ninety visitors in our first month. Isn't that a convincing result?
M: It shows interest, but not necessarily a reduction in waste. Some visitors only came to watch, and several brought objects that couldn't be repaired safely.
W: So we should count the appliances that volunteers successfully fix?
M: That's a better start. However, an item repaired on Saturday might break again on Monday. The foundation suggested contacting owners six weeks later to see whether the objects are still being used.
W: We could ask whether they would otherwise have bought replacements. That would help distinguish an actual avoided purchase from a repair to a spare item.
M: Exactly. We should also record why a repair fails. If the same inexpensive component keeps making products impossible to mend, our records could be useful to designers.
W: What about the volunteer survey? I was going to ask everyone how satisfied they were with the event.
M: Keep it, but separate it from the environmental results. Volunteers may gain skills and friendships even when a repair is unsuccessful. Those benefits deserve their own evidence.
W: This sounds like considerably more work for the front desk. We already had a queue last Saturday.
M: Then let's test a short form at two tables, rather than introducing it everywhere immediately. Owners can choose whether to leave contact details.
W: Good. I'll ask two volunteers to try the form and report any confusing questions before our next event. We can revise the application after that.

Listening script · Conversation Two
M: Professor Ellis, I've finished interviewing the former factory workers for our exhibition. Their accounts are much livelier than the company reports.
W: That's encouraging, Maya. Have you decided how to present the interviews?
M: I thought visitors could listen to people describing their first day at work. Most of them remember it very clearly, even after forty years.
W: A strong opening. But remember that vivid memories are not necessarily complete records. Someone may recall a friendly supervisor while forgetting the uncomfortable working conditions.
M: Actually, that difference appears in my interviews. Several workers praised the sense of community, although inspection records mention constant noise and poor ventilation.
W: Don't make those sources compete for a single verdict. They answer different questions. The inspection tells us about physical conditions, while the interviews reveal how people understood their working lives.
M: So I can place a short extract from the safety report beside an audio clip, and explain what each contributes?
W: Yes, provided you give enough context. Also, did every interviewee agree to have their voice used publicly?
M: They signed the general consent form before we started.
W: They still need a chance to review the particular extracts. A remark that felt harmless in a private conversation can sound quite different in a museum, especially when former colleagues might recognize the speaker.
M: I'll send them the selected clips, with the text that will appear alongside them. Should I invite them to help choose the exhibition's title as well?
W: That would be worthwhile. Just avoid promising that every suggestion will be adopted. Explain the practical limits and how the final decision will be made.
M: Understood. I want the workers to influence the exhibition, rather than appear only as voices inside headphones.
W: Then make their review part of the production schedule, not an invitation sent after everything has been printed.

Listening script · Passage One
When a city announces a programme to plant thousands of trees, the number sounds like an obvious measure of progress. Yet urban ecologist Hannah Reed argues that counting new trees tells us surprisingly little about the shade residents will actually receive.

A tree planted in a narrow pavement opening may struggle to survive if its roots lack water and space. Another, planted in a large park, may thrive but provide little protection to people waiting beside a hot bus stop. Reed therefore begins her surveys by observing where people spend time outdoors, especially during the hottest part of the day.

Her team recently worked with a neighbourhood association to compare two proposed planting sites. Residents initially preferred a broad avenue where a row of trees would look impressive. Temperature readings and walking interviews, however, revealed that the route to a nearby clinic exposed many older residents to intense afternoon heat. The association redirected its first planting effort to that route.

The project also changed the way maintenance was funded. Instead of paying contractors mainly for the number of trees delivered, the city reserved part of the payment for keeping them alive through their first three summers. Local residents could report damaged supports or dry soil, but responsibility for watering remained with the contractor.

Reed emphasizes that trees take time to grow. In particularly exposed places, temporary shelters may be needed while the canopy develops. For her, a credible cooling programme combines immediate protection with patient care, and judges its success by the conditions people experience.

Listening script · Passage Two
At Westbridge University, laboratory technicians used to receive large numbers of requests for equipment that researchers needed only occasionally. Individual departments bought their own instruments, while suitable machines stood idle in neighbouring buildings. The problem was not an absolute shortage of equipment, but a shortage of information and trust.

The university's first response was to create an online inventory. It listed every available machine, together with a contact name. Use remained disappointing. Researchers could see that a machine existed, but could not tell whether it was properly maintained, what training was necessary, or who would pay if something went wrong.

A second version of the scheme addressed those questions. Technicians recorded maintenance schedules and offered short introductory sessions. Departments agreed on a common damage policy and modest charges that covered consumables rather than generating profit. Crucially, the technicians were given working hours specifically for supporting outside users. Sharing was no longer an extra duty squeezed between their other tasks.

Within a year, bookings increased substantially, and two departments postponed purchases they had previously considered essential. The university did not treat those postponed purchases as permanent savings: demand could grow, and some instruments might eventually need replacing. It did, however, gain evidence that a service built around equipment could be more valuable than a list of equipment alone.

The organizers now interview researchers whose booking attempts fail. Those accounts may reveal inaccessible training times or unsuitable laboratory hours, problems that a rising total of successful bookings would otherwise conceal.

Listening script · Recording One
Today I want to consider a familiar phrase: scientific uncertainty. In public debate, the phrase is sometimes treated as a confession that scientists know almost nothing. In scientific work, however, describing uncertainty is often evidence that researchers understand the boundaries of what they know.

Imagine that a coastal town wants to decide how high to build a flood barrier. A research team produces a range of estimates for future water levels. The range reflects several sources of uncertainty: incomplete observations, different ways of representing physical processes, and the choices society will make about future emissions. These are not interchangeable problems, and collecting more measurements will not necessarily eliminate all of them.

An engineer who presents only the middle estimate may appear admirably clear. But if the town uses that single figure, it may overlook a less likely outcome with extremely serious consequences. The useful question is not simply which number is most probable. It is also which mistakes would be hardest to recover from, and how a decision could be adjusted as new information arrives.

One approach is to design a barrier whose foundations can support additional height later. Another is to reserve land behind it so that future construction is not blocked by new buildings. Such choices do not require waiting until uncertainty disappears. They require distinguishing commitments that can be revised from those that lock a community into one path.

Communication matters here. Giving the public a complicated graph without explaining the decision it informs is rarely enough. Nor is saying that an outcome is unlikely, since different listeners may attach very different numbers to that word. Researchers should explain what their estimates include, what they leave out, and why the remaining uncertainty matters for the particular choice.

This does not mean every decision must follow the most alarming possibility. Resources are limited, and protection has costs of its own. It means making the trade-offs visible, so that a confident presentation does not silently substitute for a reasoned decision. People can disagree about acceptable risk while still sharing an accurate understanding of the evidence.

The most responsible adviser is therefore not always the one who supplies the neatest answer. It may be the one who helps a community recognize which uncertainty can be reduced, which must be managed, and which decision will remain useful across several plausible futures.

Listening script · Recording Two
When people hear about a successful medical discovery, they usually imagine a dramatic experiment. They seldom picture someone carefully recording that a promising treatment failed to produce the expected effect. Yet those disappointing findings can be essential to scientific progress.

Suppose ten research teams independently test the same idea. Two obtain a positive result, while eight find no convincing effect. If only the two positive studies become visible, later researchers may believe the evidence is much stronger than it really is. They may repeat an unproductive approach, and reviewers may struggle to explain why apparently similar experiments lead to different conclusions.

The problem is not solved merely by asking journals to publish more negative results. A study that finds no effect may be too small, use an unreliable measure, or test an intervention that participants never actually received. To interpret the result, readers need to know what was planned, what was done, and how much difference the experiment could reasonably detect.

This is one reason for registering a study before data collection begins. Researchers specify their main question, procedures and intended analysis in a public record. Registration makes it easier to distinguish an original prediction from an interesting pattern noticed afterwards. Both can be valuable, but they should not be presented as though they provide the same kind of evidence.

A related practice is to agree on publication before the findings are known, once reviewers have judged the question and methods worthwhile. This changes the incentive: careful design becomes a reason to publish, rather than merely a preparation for a result that editors may find exciting. Researchers still have to report deviations and limitations. An advance agreement is not a certificate that every conclusion will be correct.

There are practical obstacles. Preparing detailed records takes time, and some exploratory work cannot specify every step in advance. The aim should be to make the research process visible, not to punish every reasonable change of direction. For example, an unexpected observation may justify a new experiment, provided that the new question is clearly identified.

If institutions want these practices to spread, they must also recognize the work involved. Hiring and funding decisions that reward only surprising positive findings will undermine messages about transparency. A reliable scientific record depends on rewarding contributions that help others learn, including well-supported reasons to stop pursuing an attractive idea.

Listening script · Recording Three
I study how people use public libraries, and one finding repeatedly surprises city officials. A library can be busier than ever while lending fewer books. This is not necessarily a sign that reading has become unimportant. It may show that the building is meeting needs which the lending statistics were never designed to capture.

Consider someone applying for a job online. At home, she has a phone, but no quiet space, reliable connection or keyboard. The library provides a computer, and a staff member helps her understand an unfamiliar application form. No book changes hands, yet something important has happened. If we judge the visit only by loans, the service is effectively invisible.

Libraries have responded by counting other activities: computer sessions, attendance at workshops, use of meeting rooms and requests for assistance. These figures improve the picture, but they introduce their own distortions. An introductory class may attract thirty people while a difficult request for help occupies a librarian for an hour and benefits only one person. A simple total can encourage staff to prefer activities that produce large numbers quickly.

Our research therefore combines counts with short accounts of what visitors were trying to accomplish. We ask why a particular service mattered and what alternatives were available. We also speak to people who rarely enter the library. Their absence may reflect inconvenient opening hours, inaccessible transport or uncertainty about whether the building is welcoming to them.

Importantly, we do not ask staff to collect detailed personal histories. People should be able to use a public service without explaining private difficulties. Participation in interviews is voluntary, and published examples remove identifying details. The purpose is to understand patterns of need, not to create a profile of every visitor.

One library used this approach to reconsider a planned technology room. Officials had assumed that buying more advanced devices would attract new users. Interviews instead revealed demand for basic assistance during evenings, when existing support was unavailable. The library extended staffed hours before committing to additional equipment.

The lesson reaches beyond libraries. Measures should help an institution understand its purpose, rather than quietly redefine that purpose around whatever is easiest to count. Numbers remain necessary for planning and accountability. Their value increases when they are interpreted alongside the circumstances that give them meaning, and alongside the experiences of people the current service fails to reach.

Reading Section A · Making public data usable
When organizations decide to make their records public, they often begin by asking how much information they can release. A more useful question is whether anyone outside the organization can actually understand and use it. A collection of numbers is not automatically a form of public knowledge.

For example, a transport authority may publish detailed records of bus arrivals. Without clear definitions, however, users cannot tell whether an arrival time was observed on the street or merely copied from the timetable. The distinction is [26] to anyone investigating delays. Information about missing observations is equally important, since gaps may be [27] in neighbourhoods with older monitoring equipment.

Usable data therefore require work that is less visible than building an attractive website. Staff must explain how figures were [28], preserve previous versions and provide a way for users to report errors. They must also [29] personal information before publication. Removing names alone may be insufficient when several details can be combined to identify an individual.

The most successful projects treat publication as an [30] relationship. Community groups may notice a misleading category or propose a comparison that officials had not considered. Their questions can [31] weaknesses in the original records and help improve later collection.

This process is not [32]. It takes time, and different users sometimes want incompatible things. Nevertheless, a smaller collection with reliable documentation may be more [33] than a vast collection whose origins remain obscure. Organizations should consequently [34] resources for maintenance and public support, rather than spending the entire budget on an impressive launch. Openness becomes useful when people can [35] examine the evidence behind an institution's claims.

A) allocate
B) collected
C) concentrated
D) essential
E) expose
F) independently
G) ongoing
H) productive
I) protect
J) straightforward
K) abandoned
L) casual
M) exhausted
N) reverse
O) temporary

Reading Section B · What makes a shared workshop accessible?
[A] Across many cities, unused shops and warehouses are being converted into shared workshops. Members pay a small fee to use sewing machines, woodworking tools or digital equipment that they could not afford individually. Supporters describe these places as engines of creativity. Yet the most interesting question is not how many impressive objects leave the building. It is whether people who arrive without technical confidence can gradually become capable participants. A workshop full of expensive machines can remain inaccessible even when its front door is open.

[B] The obstacles begin before anyone touches a tool. A website may advertise a workshop as suitable for everyone while filling its instructions with unfamiliar abbreviations. Photographs may show only experienced users working alone, leaving newcomers unsure whether asking for help is acceptable. Some organizers have therefore invited first-time visitors to review their introductory information. Their questions reveal assumptions that regular members no longer notice, such as whether protective equipment is provided and whether a person needs a finished project before joining.

[C] Price is another obvious barrier, but reducing the membership fee does not remove every cost. Materials, travel and childcare can make an apparently affordable evening session impossible. One workshop created a small materials fund so that beginners could practise without worrying that a mistake would waste supplies they had paid for. Another moved some introductory sessions to weekend afternoons after parents explained why late evenings were difficult. Both changes resulted from asking who was absent, rather than surveying existing members alone.

[D] Once visitors enter, the way assistance is offered matters. In an early observation study, instructors frequently took a difficult task out of a beginner's hands and completed it quickly. The immediate problem disappeared, but the learner had little opportunity to understand the solution. A revised approach asked instructors to demonstrate on a separate piece of material, then return the task to the learner. Sessions became slightly slower, yet participants were better able to repeat the procedure independently on their next visit.

[E] Safety cannot depend solely on people feeling comfortable enough to ask questions. Tools differ in the risks they create, so a single general induction is rarely sufficient. Several workshops now issue permissions for specific machines after practical demonstrations. Experienced members must follow the same process as newcomers when using an unfamiliar machine. The point is not to create a hierarchy of prestigious badges, organizers explain, but to make the limits of each person's training visible to everyone sharing the space.

[F] The social atmosphere can also exclude people unintentionally. A group of long-standing members may enjoy discussing complicated projects in technical language. To an outsider, however, the conversation can suggest that expertise is a condition of belonging. At one workshop, a weekly repair table changed this pattern. People brought ordinary household objects and described what had gone wrong. The shared effort of investigating a broken lamp created a natural reason for beginners and specialists to talk, without requiring anyone to present themselves as an expert.

[G] Sharing equipment creates responsibilities that are easy to overlook. Someone must check blades, replace filters, order consumables and make sure emergency exits stay clear. In volunteer-run spaces, this work often falls repeatedly to the same small group. When it is treated as invisible generosity, reliable helpers can become exhausted. A transparent maintenance schedule allows members to see how much work is required and to contribute appropriate tasks. It also helps committees decide which duties need paid staff rather than another appeal for volunteers.

[H] Some funders judge workshops by the number of businesses launched or products sold. Those outcomes are relevant to certain projects, but they capture only part of the activity. A retired member who learns to repair clothing may never establish a company. A teenager who discovers that an unsuccessful design can be improved may produce nothing marketable that month. Both can gain something valuable. Organizers increasingly combine numerical reports with short accounts of changes in confidence, skills and relationships, while avoiding claims that every pleasant experience is a measurable economic benefit.

[I] There is a temptation to collect extensive information to demonstrate those wider benefits. Yet people may attend a workshop precisely because it offers relief from institutions that continually assess them. One project stopped asking visitors to record their employment status after several said the question felt intrusive. Instead, it used voluntary interviews with clear explanations of how responses would be stored and quoted. Scientists reconstruct past climates using evidence preserved in tree rings, sediments and ice. These natural archives do not contain temperature readings in the ordinary sense. The strongest reconstruction is not necessarily the one with the sharpest-looking line, but the one whose claims remain credible when its assumptions are made visible.

blocks.title: Writing task and assessment knowledge
blocks.text:
For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay that begins with the sentence “Learning to question a popular idea is an essential part of education.” You may give examples to support your views. You should write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words. Write your essay on Answer Sheet 1.
A successful essay develops a clear position, explains why popularity alone is insufficient evidence, uses a specific relevant example, and connects independent judgment with responsible evaluation of evidence. Different defensible positions and examples are acceptable.

blocks.title: Listening script · Conversation One
blocks.text:
W: You look worried, Ben. Did the community foundation reject our repair café proposal?
M: No, they actually liked the idea. But before releasing the grant, they want evidence that the café changes what people do, rather than simply attracting visitors.
W: We recorded ninety visitors in our first month. Isn't that a convincing result?
M: It shows interest, but not necessarily a reduction in waste. Some visitors only came to watch, and several brought objects that couldn't be repaired safely.
W: So we should count the appliances that volunteers successfully fix?
M: That's a better start. However, an item repaired on Saturday might break again on Monday. The foundation suggested contacting owners six weeks later to see whether the objects are still being used.
W: We could ask whether they would otherwise have bought replacements. That would help distinguish an actual avoided purchase from a repair to a spare item.
M: Exactly. We should also record why a repair fails. If the same inexpensive component keeps making products impossible to mend, our records could be useful to designers.
W: What about the volunteer survey? I was going to ask everyone how satisfied they were with the event.
M: Keep it, but separate it from the environmental results. Volunteers may gain skills and friendships even when a repair is unsuccessful. Those benefits deserve their own evidence.
W: This sounds like considerably more work for the front desk. We already had a queue last Saturday.
M: Then let's test a short form at two tables, rather than introducing it everywhere immediately. Owners can choose whether to leave contact details.
W: Good. I'll ask two volunteers to try the form and report any confusing questions before our next event. We can revise the application after that.

blocks.title: Listening script · Conversation Two
blocks.text:
M: Professor Ellis, I've finished interviewing the former factory workers for our exhibition. Their accounts are much livelier than the company reports.
W: That's encouraging, Maya. Have you decided how to present the interviews?
M: I thought visitors could listen to people describing their first day at work. Most of them remember it very clearly, even after forty years.
W: A strong opening. But remember that vivid memories are not necessarily complete records. Someone may recall a friendly supervisor while forgetting the uncomfortable working conditions.
M: Actually, that difference appears in my interviews. Several workers praised the sense of community, although inspection records mention constant noise and poor ventilation.
W: Don't make those sources compete for a single verdict. They answer different questions. The inspection tells us about physical conditions, while the interviews reveal how people understood their working lives.
M: So I can place a short extract from the safety report beside an audio clip, and explain what each contributes?
W: Yes, provided you give enough context. Also, did every interviewee agree to have their voice used publicly?
M: They signed the general consent form before we started.
W: They still need a chance to review the particular extracts. A remark that felt harmless in a private conversation can sound quite different in a museum, especially when former colleagues might recognize the speaker.
M: I'll send them the selected clips, with the text that will appear alongside them. Should I invite them to help choose the exhibition's title as well?
W: That would be worthwhile. Just avoid promising that every suggestion will be adopted. Explain the practical limits and how the final decision will be made.
M: Understood. I want the workers to influence the exhibition, rather than appear only as voices inside headphones.
W: Then make their review part of the production schedule, not an invitation sent after everything has been printed.

blocks.title: Listening script · Passage One
blocks.text:
When a city announces a programme to plant thousands of trees, the number sounds like an obvious measure of progress. Yet urban ecologist Hannah Reed argues that counting new trees tells us surprisingly little about the shade residents will actually receive.

A tree planted in a narrow pavement opening may struggle to survive if its roots lack water and space. Another, planted in a large park, may thrive but provide little protection to people waiting beside a hot bus stop. Reed therefore begins her surveys by observing where people spend time outdoors, especially during the hottest part of the day.

Her team recently worked with a neighbourhood association to compare two proposed planting sites. Residents initially preferred a broad avenue where a row of trees would look impressive. Temperature readings and walking interviews, however, revealed that the route to a nearby clinic exposed many older residents to intense afternoon heat. The association redirected its first planting effort to that route.

The project also changed the way maintenance was funded. Instead of paying contractors mainly for the number of trees delivered, the city reserved part of the payment for keeping them alive through their first three summers. Local residents could report damaged supports or dry soil, but responsibility for watering remained with the contractor.

Reed emphasizes that trees take time to grow. In particularly exposed places, temporary shelters may be needed while the canopy develops. For her, a credible cooling programme combines immediate protection with patient care, and judges its success by the conditions people experience.

blocks.title: Listening script · Passage Two
blocks.text:
At Westbridge University, laboratory technicians used to receive large numbers of requests for equipment that researchers needed only occasionally. Individual departments bought their own instruments, while suitable machines stood idle in neighbouring buildings. The problem was not an absolute shortage of equipment, but a shortage of information and trust.

The university's first response was to create an online inventory. It listed every available machine, together with a contact name. Use remained disappointing. Researchers could see that a machine existed, but could not tell whether it was properly maintained, what training was necessary, or who would pay if something went wrong.

A second version of the scheme addressed those questions. Technicians recorded maintenance schedules and offered short introductory sessions. Departments agreed on a common damage policy and modest charges that covered consumables rather than generating profit. Crucially, the technicians were given working hours specifically for supporting outside users. Sharing was no longer an extra duty squeezed between their other tasks.

Within a year, bookings increased substantially, and two departments postponed purchases they had previously considered essential. The university did not treat those postponed purchases as permanent savings: demand could grow, and some instruments might eventually need replacing. It did, however, gain evidence that a service built around equipment could be more valuable than a list of equipment alone.

The organizers now interview researchers whose booking attempts fail. Those accounts may reveal inaccessible training times or unsuitable laboratory hours, problems that a rising total of successful bookings would otherwise conceal.

blocks.title: Listening script · Recording One
blocks.text:
Today I want to consider a familiar phrase: scientific uncertainty. In public debate, the phrase is sometimes treated as a confession that scientists know almost nothing. In scientific work, however, describing uncertainty is often evidence that researchers understand the boundaries of what they know.

Imagine that a coastal town wants to decide how high to build a flood barrier. A research team produces a range of estimates for future water levels. The range reflects several sources of uncertainty: incomplete observations, different ways of representing physical processes, and the choices society will make about future emissions. These are not interchangeable problems, and collecting more measurements will not necessarily eliminate all of them.

An engineer who presents only the middle estimate may appear admirably clear. But if the town uses that single figure, it may overlook a less likely outcome with extremely serious consequences. The useful question is not simply which number is most probable. It is also which mistakes would be hardest to recover from, and how a decision could be adjusted as new information arrives.

One approach is to design a barrier whose foundations can support additional height later. Another is to reserve land behind it so that future construction is not blocked by new buildings. Such choices do not require waiting until uncertainty disappears. They require distinguishing commitments that can be revised from those that lock a community into one path.

Communication matters here. Giving the public a complicated graph without explaining the decision it informs is rarely enough. Nor is saying that an outcome is unlikely, since different listeners may attach very different numbers to that word. Researchers should explain what their estimates include, what they leave out, and why the remaining uncertainty matters for the particular choice.

This does not mean every decision must follow the most alarming possibility. Resources are limited, and protection has costs of its own. It means making the trade-offs visible, so that a confident presentation does not silently substitute for a reasoned decision. People can disagree about acceptable risk while still sharing an accurate understanding of the evidence.

The most responsible adviser is therefore not always the one who supplies the neatest answer. It may be the one who helps a community recognize which uncertainty can be reduced, which must be managed, and which decision will remain useful across several plausible futures.

blocks.title: Listening script · Recording Two
blocks.text:
When people hear about a successful medical discovery, they usually imagine a dramatic experiment. They seldom picture someone carefully recording that a promising treatment failed to produce the expected effect. Yet those disappointing findings can be essential to scientific progress.

Suppose ten research teams independently test the same idea. Two obtain a positive result, while eight find no convincing effect. If only the two positive studies become visible, later researchers may believe the evidence is much stronger than it really is. They may repeat an unproductive approach, and reviewers may struggle to explain why apparently similar experiments lead to different conclusions.

The problem is not solved merely by asking journals to publish more negative results. A study that finds no effect may be too small, use an unreliable measure, or test an intervention that participants never actually received. To interpret the result, readers need to know what was planned, what was done, and how much difference the experiment could reasonably detect.

This is one reason for registering a study before data collection begins. Researchers specify their main question, procedures and intended analysis in a public record. Registration makes it easier to distinguish an original prediction from an interesting pattern noticed afterwards. Both can be valuable, but they should not be presented as though they provide the same kind of evidence.

A related practice is to agree on publication before the findings are known, once reviewers have judged the question and methods worthwhile. This changes the incentive: careful design becomes a reason to publish, rather than merely a preparation for a result that editors may find exciting. Researchers still have to report deviations and limitations. An advance agreement is not a certificate that every conclusion will be correct.

There are practical obstacles. Preparing detailed records takes time, and some exploratory work cannot specify every step in advance. The aim should be to make the research process visible, not to punish every reasonable change of direction. For example, an unexpected observation may justify a new experiment, provided that the new question is clearly identified.

If institutions want these practices to spread, they must also recognize the work involved. Hiring and funding decisions that reward only surprising positive findings will undermine messages about transparency. A reliable scientific record depends on rewarding contributions that help others learn, including well-supported reasons to stop pursuing an attractive idea.

blocks.title: Listening script · Recording Three
blocks.text:
I study how people use public libraries, and one finding repeatedly surprises city officials. A library can be busier than ever while lending fewer books. This is not necessarily a sign that reading has become unimportant. It may show that the building is meeting needs which the lending statistics were never designed to capture.

Consider someone applying for a job online. At home, she has a phone, but no quiet space, reliable connection or keyboard. The library provides a computer, and a staff member helps her understand an unfamiliar application form. No book changes hands, yet something important has happened. If we judge the visit only by loans, the service is effectively invisible.

Libraries have responded by counting other activities: computer sessions, attendance at workshops, use of meeting rooms and requests for assistance. These figures improve the picture, but they introduce their own distortions. An introductory class may attract thirty people while a difficult request for help occupies a librarian for an hour and benefits only one person. A simple total can encourage staff to prefer activities that produce large numbers quickly.

Our research therefore combines counts with short accounts of what visitors were trying to accomplish. We ask why a particular service mattered and what alternatives were available. We also speak to people who rarely enter the library. Their absence may reflect inconvenient opening hours, inaccessible transport or uncertainty about whether the building is welcoming to them.

Importantly, we do not ask staff to collect detailed personal histories. People should be able to use a public service without explaining private difficulties. Participation in interviews is voluntary, and published examples remove identifying details. The purpose is to understand patterns of need, not to create a profile of every visitor.

One library used this approach to reconsider a planned technology room. Officials had assumed that buying more advanced devices would attract new users. Interviews instead revealed demand for basic assistance during evenings, when existing support was unavailable. The library extended staffed hours before committing to additional equipment.

The lesson reaches beyond libraries. Measures should help an institution understand its purpose, rather than quietly redefine that purpose around whatever is easiest to count. Numbers remain necessary for planning and accountability. Their value increases when they are interpreted alongside the circumstances that give them meaning, and alongside the experiences of people the current service fails to reach.

blocks.title: Reading Section A · Making public data usable
blocks.text:
When organizations decide to make their records public, they often begin by asking how much information they can release. A more useful question is whether anyone outside the organization can actually understand and use it. A collection of numbers is not automatically a form of public knowledge.

For example, a transport authority may publish detailed records of bus arrivals. Without clear definitions, however, users cannot tell whether an arrival time was observed on the street or merely copied from the timetable. The distinction is [26] to anyone investigating delays. Information about missing observations is equally important, since gaps may be [27] in neighbourhoods with older monitoring equipment.

Usable data therefore require work that is less visible than building an attractive website. Staff must explain how figures were [28], preserve previous versions and provide a way for users to report errors. They must also [29] personal information before publication. Removing names alone may be insufficient when several details can be combined to identify an individual.

The most successful projects treat publication as an [30] relationship. Community groups may notice a misleading category or propose a comparison that officials had not considered. Their questions can [31] weaknesses in the original records and help improve later collection.

This process is not [32]. It takes time, and different users sometimes want incompatible things. Nevertheless, a smaller collection with reliable documentation may be more [33] than a vast collection whose origins remain obscure. Organizations should consequently [34] resources for maintenance and public support, rather than spending the entire budget on an impressive launch. Openness becomes useful when people can [35] examine the evidence behind an institution's claims.

Providing that chain makes a reconstruction open to examination and improvement. It also allows researchers from other fields to ask whether the record is suitable for their particular question. The strongest reconstruction is not necessarily the one with the sharpest-looking line, but the one whose claims remain credible when its assumptions are made visible.

blocks.title: Translation task · Urban renewal
blocks.text: 近年来，中国许多城市开始改造旧工业区。一些曾经闲置的厂房被改建为图书馆、艺术空间和面向公众的科学教育中心。这种做法既保留了城市发展的历史记忆，也为居民提供了新的公共活动场所。然而，改造并不只是修缮建筑外观。规划者还需要改善公共交通，方便老年人和残障人士使用设施，并考虑周边居民的实际需求。有些项目邀请居民参与设计，了解他们希望保留什么、改变什么。随着人们更重视生活品质，如何让历史建筑持续服务于社区，已成为城市更新中的一个重要课题。

questions.prompt: Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay that begins with the sentence “Learning to question a popular idea is an essential part of education.” You may give examples to support your views. You should write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words. Write your essay on Answer Sheet 1.
questions.solution:
Learning to question a popular idea is an essential part of education. When students discover that agreement does not guarantee accuracy, they begin to replace borrowed opinions with informed judgments.

Consider the widespread belief that studying for longer always produces better results. A student may follow this advice by staying up late every night, only to find that exhaustion damages concentration. By comparing study records and learning about sleep, the student can develop a more effective routine. Questioning the original idea leads to improvement because it creates an opportunity to examine evidence.

However, independent thinking does not mean rejecting every widely accepted view. Some ideas are popular precisely because they have survived careful investigation. Education should therefore teach students to ask useful questions, consult reliable sources and revise their conclusions when stronger evidence appears. Listening respectfully to others remains part of this process.

Schools can encourage these habits through discussions in which students explain both their claims and their reasons. The goal is to develop people who can make thoughtful decisions when neither popularity nor personal confidence provides a sufficient guide.

sections.instructions:
Section A
Directions: In this section, there is a passage with ten blanks. Select one word for each blank from the list of choices given below. Each choice is identified by a letter. Mark the corresponding letter for each item on Answer Sheet 2. You may not use any of the words in the list more than once.

source.title: Reading Section A · Making public data usable
source.exact:
When organizations decide to make their records public, they often begin by asking how much information they can release. A more useful question is whether anyone outside the organization can actually understand and use it. A collection of numbers is not automatically a form of public knowledge.

For example, a transport authority may publish detailed records of bus arrivals. Without clear definitions, however, users cannot tell whether an arrival time was observed on the street or merely copied from the timetable. The distinction is [26] to anyone investigating delays. Information about missing observations is equally important, since gaps may be [27] in neighbourhoods with older monitoring equipment.

Usable data therefore require work that is less visible than building an attractive website. Staff must explain how figures were [28], preserve previous versions and provide a way for users to report errors. They must also [29] personal information before publication. Removing names alone may be insufficient when several details can be combined to identify an individual.

The most successful projects treat publication as an [30] relationship. Community groups may notice a misleading category or propose a comparison that officials had not considered. Their questions can [31] weaknesses in the original records and help improve later collection.

This process is not [32]. It takes time, and different users sometimes want incompatible things. Nevertheless, a smaller collection with reliable documentation may be more [33] than a vast collection whose origins remain obscure. Organizations should consequently [34] resources for maintenance and public support, rather than spending the entire budget on an impressive launch. Openness becomes useful when people can [35] examine the evidence behind an institution's claims.

Without clear definitions, however, users cannot tell whether an arrival time was observed on the street or merely copied from the timetable. The distinction is [26] to anyone investigating delays. Information about missing observations is equally important, since gaps may be [27] in neighbourhoods with older monitoring equipment.

Usable data therefore require work that is less visible than building an attractive website. Staff must explain how figures were [28], preserve previous versions and provide a way for users to report errors. They must also [29] personal information before publication. Removing names alone may be insufficient when several details can be combined to identify an individual.

The most successful projects treat publication as an [30] relationship. Community groups may notice a misleading category or propose a comparison that officials had not considered. Their questions can [31] weaknesses in the original records and help improve later collection.

This process is not [32]. It takes time, and different users sometimes want incompatible things. Nevertheless, a smaller collection with reliable documentation may be more [33] than a vast collection whose origins remain obscure. Organizations should consequently [34] resources for maintenance and public support, rather than spending the entire budget on an impressive launch. stimulus.title: What makes a shared workshop accessible?
stimulus.text:
[A] Across many cities, unused shops and warehouses are being converted into shared workshops. Members pay a small fee to use sewing machines, woodworking tools or digital equipment that they could not afford individually. Supporters describe these places as engines of creativity. Yet the most interesting question is not how many impressive objects leave the building. It is whether people who arrive without technical confidence can gradually become capable participants. A workshop full of expensive machines can remain inaccessible even when its front door is open.

[B] The obstacles begin before anyone touches a tool. A website may advertise a workshop as suitable for everyone while filling its instructions with unfamiliar abbreviations. Photographs may show only experienced users working alone, leaving newcomers unsure whether asking for help is acceptable. Some organizers have therefore invited first-time visitors to review their introductory information. Their questions reveal assumptions that regular members no longer notice, such as whether protective equipment is provided and whether a person needs a finished project before joining.

[C] Price is another obvious barrier, but reducing the membership fee does not remove every cost. Materials, travel and childcare can make an apparently affordable evening session impossible. One workshop created a small materials fund so that beginners could practise without worrying that a mistake would waste supplies they had paid for. Another moved some introductory sessions to weekend afternoons after parents explained why late evenings were difficult. Both changes resulted from asking who was absent, rather than surveying existing members alone.

[D] Once visitors enter, the way assistance is offered matters. In an early observation study, instructors frequently took a difficult task out of a beginner's hands and completed it quickly. The immediate problem disappeared, but the learner had little opportunity to understand the solution. A revised approach asked instructors to demonstrate on a separate piece of material, then return the task to the learner. Sessions became slightly slower, yet participants were better able to repeat the procedure independently on their next visit.

[E] Safety cannot depend solely on people feeling comfortable enough to ask questions. Tools differ in the risks they create, so a single general induction is rarely sufficient. Several workshops now issue permissions for specific machines after practical demonstrations. Experienced members must follow the same process as newcomers when using an unfamiliar machine. The point is not to create a hierarchy of prestigious badges, organizers explain, but to make the limits of each person's training visible to everyone sharing the space.

[F] The social atmosphere can also exclude people unintentionally. A group of long-standing members may enjoy discussing complicated projects in technical language. To an outsider, however, the conversation can suggest that expertise is a condition of belonging. At one workshop, a weekly repair table changed this pattern. People brought ordinary household objects and described what had gone wrong. The shared effort of investigating a broken lamp created a natural reason for beginners and specialists to talk, without requiring anyone to present themselves as an expert.

[G] Sharing equipment creates responsibilities that are easy to overlook. Someone must check blades, replace filters, order consumables and make sure emergency exits stay clear. In volunteer-run spaces, this work often falls repeatedly to the same small group. When it is treated as invisible generosity, reliable helpers can become exhausted. A transparent maintenance schedule allows members to see how much work is required and to contribute appropriate tasks. It also helps committees decide which duties need paid staff rather than another appeal for volunteers.

[H] Some funders judge workshops by the number of businesses launched or products sold. Those outcomes are relevant to certain projects, but they capture only part of the activity. A retired member who learns to repair clothing may never establish a company. A teenager who discovers that an unsuccessful design can be improved may produce nothing marketable that month. Both can gain something valuable. Organizers increasingly combine numerical reports with short accounts of changes in confidence, skills and relationships, while avoiding claims that every pleasant experience is a measurable economic benefit.

[I] There is a temptation to collect extensive information to demonstrate those wider benefits. Yet people may attend a workshop precisely because it offers relief from institutions that continually assess them. One project stopped asking visitors to record their employment status after several said the question felt intrusive. Instead, it used voluntary interviews with clear explanations of how responses would be stored and quoted. Evaluating access should not turn participation into an obligation to disclose personal circumstances that have little relevance to using a tool.

[J] Connections with schools can broaden access, but a brief class visit is not the same as sustained participation. Students may enjoy a demonstration and then find no affordable route back. A partnership in one town therefore included a return pass, travel support and a named contact who could answer questions after the school session. Teachers also discussed workshop activities in later lessons. The arrangement treated the visit as the beginning of a relationship, rather than an isolated event whose success was measured by a group photograph.

[K] Digital tools introduce a different challenge. A machine may remain physically sound while the commercial software needed to operate it becomes unavailable or unaffordable. Workshops that depend on a single vendor can lose capabilities without any visible mechanical failure. Some now preserve exportable design files, document alternative software and consider the future availability of spare parts before buying equipment. The cheapest purchase price may offer poor value if continued use depends on subscriptions that a small organization cannot reliably maintain.

[L] Not every member wants to design something from the beginning. Patterns and shared instructions can provide a useful starting point, especially when they explain why a procedure works. However, copying a finished model without understanding its assumptions may lead to failure when materials or dimensions change. Good documentation therefore records tests, common errors and conditions under which a design should not be used. It makes knowledge easier to adapt, rather than merely producing identical objects more quickly.

[M] As workshops become popular, booking systems can quietly change who gets access. Confident members reserve desirable times weeks ahead, while people with unpredictable work schedules struggle to commit. One space reserved a portion of each week's machine hours for bookings made only a day in advance. It monitored whether this actually increased access for occasional users before expanding the policy. A formally equal rule, the committee learned, can have unequal effects when members have very different control over their time.

[N] The relationship with the surrounding neighbourhood also needs attention. A busy workshop may attract visitors who support local cafés, yet noise, deliveries and evening traffic can inconvenience nearby residents. Regular conversations with neighbours helped one organization relocate a noisy extraction unit and alter delivery hours. These negotiations were easier because the workshop had established a contact route before receiving a formal complaint. Community value was treated as a relationship to maintain, rather than a label the organization could award itself.

[O] Shared workshops will not replace professional manufacturing or remove every inequality in technical education. Their contribution is more specific: they can give people repeated opportunities to try, ask, fail and improve with others. Realizing that contribution requires attention to language, time, care, maintenance and the distribution of authority. Machines make certain activities possible. The arrangements around those machines determine who can take advantage of them, and whether an initial invitation develops into a lasting opportunity to learn.

stimulus.text:
A growing number of employers encourage staff to propose improvements to the way work is organized. Suggestion platforms promise to make good ideas visible regardless of an employee's seniority. But an idea can be visible without being heard. The difficult part is often what happens after someone presses “submit”.

In a study of several service organizations, researchers found that employees watched the treatment of earlier suggestions before deciding whether to contribute. A rejection accompanied by a clear explanation did not necessarily discourage participation. Silence did. When proposals disappeared into an online system without acknowledgment, staff concluded that contributing was unlikely to be worth the effort. The platform preserved their words while leaving the decision process inaccessible. Even experienced employees who had once supported the programme began to advise new colleagues against spending time on detailed submissions.

Managers sometimes defended slow responses by pointing to the large volume of suggestions. This was a real constraint, but it also revealed a problem in the programme's design. Organizations had invested in collecting ideas without allocating time for evaluating them. A tool intended to distribute influence instead created another channel through which a few managers controlled attention. Inviting more contributions intensified the bottleneck.

One organization changed its procedure. Teams discussed proposals during scheduled meetings, recorded reasons for accepting or rejecting them, and identified who could authorize an experiment. Small trials were given modest resources and a review date. Not every suggestion was adopted, but staff could see how a decision had been reached and what evidence might justify reconsidering it. Proposals also improved because contributors learned which practical details were needed.

This approach had limits. Public discussion could expose less confident employees to criticism, and some suggestions concerned problems that colleagues were reluctant to acknowledge. The organization therefore retained a confidential route and trained meeting facilitators to separate criticism of an idea from judgments about its author. Participation required more than making a microphone available.

The researchers argue that the quality of a suggestion scheme should not be judged solely by the number of ideas submitted. A sudden increase may reflect enthusiasm, but it may also create unrealistic expectations if the institution cannot respond. More useful questions concern whose proposals receive attention, whether decisions are explained, and whether employees can influence the criteria by which ideas are assessed. An organization learns from its staff when it builds a credible path from speaking to consideration, rather than treating expression itself as evidence of influence.

Small trials were given modest resources and a review date. Not every suggestion was adopted, but staff could see how a decision had been reached and what evidence might justify reconsidering it. Proposals also improved because contributors learned which practical details were needed.

This approach had limits. Public discussion could expose less confident employees to criticism, and some suggestions concerned problems that colleagues were reluctant to acknowledge. The organization therefore retained a confidential route and trained meeting facilitators to separate criticism of an idea from judgments about its author. Participation required more than making a microphone available.

The researchers argue that the quality of a suggestion scheme should not be judged solely by the number of ideas submitted. A sudden increase may reflect enthusiasm, but it may also create unrealistic expectations if the institution cannot respond. More useful questions concern whose proposals receive attention, whether decisions are explained, and whether employees can influence the criteria by which ideas are assessed. An organization learns from its staff when it builds a credible path from speaking to consideration, rather than treating expression itself as evidence of influence.

stimulus.text:
Scientists reconstruct past climates using evidence preserved in tree rings, sediments and ice. These natural archives do not contain temperature readings in the ordinary sense. Instead, researchers interpret physical or chemical features that respond to environmental conditions. The resulting records are valuable precisely because they extend beyond the period covered by instruments, but using them requires attention to how each archive was formed.

Consider a lake sediment core. Material settles on the lake floor year after year, carrying traces of organisms, soil and human activity. A change in one chemical component may reflect a wetter climate. It might also result from a new farming practice upstream. Treating every change as a direct climate signal would turn a complicated environmental history into an artificially simple graph.

Researchers address this problem by examining several indicators and comparing sites. If independent archives show a similar pattern, confidence in a regional explanation increases. Agreement is not a substitute for understanding the mechanisms, however. Two indicators may be affected by the same local disturbance, so their apparent independence must be checked. More records do not automatically mean more distinct evidence.

Timing creates another challenge. The age of sediment at a particular depth is usually estimated rather than known exactly. A dramatic event in one core may appear to precede an event elsewhere, but the estimated age ranges can overlap. Claiming that the first event caused the second solely on the basis of their central dates would give the chronology more precision than the evidence supports. Researchers therefore examine how conclusions change across plausible age estimates.

These qualifications sometimes make reconstructed histories look less decisive than a single smooth curve. Yet showing a range can be a scientific achievement: it identifies which features remain consistent and which depend on uncertain assumptions. A broad, persistent cooling across many records may be robust even when the exact starting year cannot be established. Different questions require different levels of chronological detail.

The practical implication is that natural archives should be treated as evidence produced through a chain of reasoning. Readers need to know the measurements, the interpretation linking them to climate, and the uncertainties in assigning dates. Providing that chain makes a reconstruction open to examination and improvement. It also allows researchers from other fields to ask whether the record is suitable for their particular question. The strongest reconstruction is not necessarily the one with the sharpest-looking line, but the one whose claims remain credible when its assumptions are made visible.

sections.title: Translation
sections.instructions: Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to translate a passage from Chinese into English. You should write your answer on Answer Sheet 2.

questions.prompt: 近年来，中国许多城市开始改造旧工业区。一些曾经闲置的厂房被改建为图书馆、艺术空间和面向公众的科学教育中心。这种做法既保留了城市发展的历史记忆，也为居民提供了新的公共活动场所。然而，改造并不只是修缮建筑外观。规划者还需要改善公共交通，方便老年人和残障人士使用设施，并考虑周边居民的实际需求。有些项目邀请居民参与设计，了解他们希望保留什么、改变什么。随着人们更重视生活品质，如何让历史建筑持续服务于社区，已成为城市更新中的一个重要课题。
questions.solution: In recent years, many Chinese cities have begun redeveloping old industrial areas. Some factories that once stood idle have been converted into libraries, art spaces and science education centres open to the public. This approach preserves the historical memory of urban development while providing residents with new places for public activities. However, redevelopment involves more than improving the appearance of buildings. Planners also need to improve public transport, make the facilities accessible to older people and people with disabilities, and consider the practical needs of nearby residents. Some projects invite residents to participate in the design process to learn what they wish to retain and what they hope to change. As people place greater value on the quality of everyday life, ensuring that historic buildings continue to serve their communities has become an important issue in urban renewal.
questions.explanation: 15分自评。信息完整与准确8分：城市改造旧工业区1；闲置厂房改为三类公共空间2；保留历史并增加活动场所1；不只修外观及交通/无障碍/居民需求2；居民参与、保留与改变1；生活品质与持续服务社区这一课题1。句法、逻辑和衔接4分；词汇、拼写、标点3分。可采用不同的准确自然译法；不要求逐字对应参考译文。
